California's Friant Division · research atlas

Can wet-year water insure agriculture against the next drought?

This atlas examines whether an additional acre-foot of wet-year Class 2 delivery is followed by less groundwater decline, fewer new wells, and less agricultural adjustment during the next drought.

Research question

Do wet-year Class 2 deliveries reduce groundwater stress and agricultural adjustment in the next drought?

Start here

How Friant water works

USBR makes water available to contractors. The contractor then schedules deliveries and distributes water under its local rules. A federal allocation percentage is therefore not the same as water received by a farm.

Class 1

The more dependable contractual tier

Class 1 refers to the first block of Friant supply defined in contractor agreements. During shortage years, USBR applies the operative Class 1 percentage to each contractor's verified contractual quantity.

It is more dependable than Class 2, but it can still be reduced. Class 1 was announced at zero in 2014 and 2015.

Class 2

The lower-reliability, wet-year tier

Class 2 becomes available after higher-priority requirements and operating constraints are considered. It is often zero in dry years and can be substantial in wetter years.

Its research value is intertemporal: districts may use wet-year deliveries for recharge or other authorised uses before a later drought.

From reservoir conditions to water at the farm

1Hydrology and operationsReservoir inflow, storage, legal requirements and system constraints
2USBR announcementClass 1 and Class 2 percentages are announced and can be revised
3Contractor availabilityThe percentage is applied to the contractor's operative quantity
4Delivery scheduleThe district requests when and how much water it plans to receive
5Canal deliveryWater is moved through federal canals to district turnouts
6Local responseDistricts and farms distribute water, pump groundwater, recharge, fallow or change crops
Important: allocation minus delivery is an accounting difference—not automatic proof of an unmet request. Delivery schedules, transfers, exchanges, carry-over and water-type ledgers are needed before calling it a shortfall.

Farmland and cultivation

What is cultivated across the mapped Friant landscape?

The crop layer is the California Department of Water Resources 2023 statewide crop-mapping product clipped to the study area. It identifies mapped crop and land-use units. It does not identify farm ownership or legal parcel boundaries.

Mapped area

Crop and land-use groups

2023 snapshot

Urban/developed and other non-crop classes are retained so the clipped landscape is not misrepresented as farm land.

How to read this

Fields are not farms

One farm may contain several mapped fields, and one field may not correspond to an ownership parcel. Use the layer to describe crop composition and exposed land, not the number or identity of farmers.

Groundwater-potential class is a screening result, not a measurement of pumping, legal access or available groundwater volume.

Groundwater and physical context

Separate maps show what each theme contributes

Elevation, slope, drainage, geology, landform, soil, rainfall, aquifer setting, groundwater depth and land use describe different parts of the physical system. They can support a groundwater-potential screening map, but they do not measure groundwater availability by themselves.

Terrain

Elevation

1

Standardise

Place each theme on a common ordinal scale so unlike units can be compared.

2

Weight

Apply transparent pilot weights drawn from hydrogeologic reasoning, then test alternative weight sets.

3

Combine

Create a relative screening score and classify it into very low to very high zones.

4

Validate

Compare scores with observed groundwater levels, wells or recharge evidence before using the index in inference.

Do not interpret the groundwater-potential map as groundwater availability. Availability requires storage, saturated thickness, aquifer properties, pumping, recharge, water quality, legal constraints and time-specific groundwater levels.

Descriptive analysis

What the assembled data can show now

The present package supports transparent measurement of policy exposure, observed deliveries, well-completion records, groundwater monitoring coverage, crop composition and physical context. It does not yet identify a causal drought-insurance effect.

A

Allocation history

Annual Class 1 and Class 2 shares identify system-wide policy exposure and the dates of severe curtailment.

B

Observed deliveries

Contractor-year delivery records identify the quantity and timing of wet-year Class 2 exposure, subject to ledger classification.

C

Well investment

Well-completion reports provide a dated measure of new drilling activity; a report is not the same as extraction.

D

Groundwater conditions

Monitoring records can trace groundwater depth, but spatial coverage and measurement timing differ across districts.

Empirical feasibility

A feasible descriptive panel; a causal design still needs stronger identification

155primary contractor–wet-year episodes
17contractors represented
7later drought years
145episodes with well and groundwater outcomes

Step 1 · Exposure

Measure wet-year Class 2 delivery

Build contractor-year exposure from observed Class 2 deliveries, not from the allocation percentage alone.

Step 2 · Horizon

Identify the next drought

Link each wet-year exposure to a defined later year in which the final Class 1 allocation falls below 100%.

Step 3 · Outcomes

Measure adjustment

Compare groundwater depth, well-completion records, fallowing and crop outcomes during the later drought.

Step 4 · Identification

Address selection

Class 2 uptake is not random. The design must account for recharge capacity, crop mix, groundwater access, hydrology, district traits and prior trends.

Available now

  • Allocation shares and revisions
  • Contractor delivery ledgers
  • DWR well-completion records
  • Groundwater monitoring points
  • 2023 crop/LULC snapshot
  • Rainfall and physical layers

Needed for the strongest study

  • Verified operative contract quantities and amendments
  • District schedules, transfers, exchanges and carry-over
  • Groundwater extraction or pumping-energy records
  • Annual crop/fallowing and production outcomes
  • Recharge-facility and banking operations
  • A pre-specified causal identification strategy
Central limitation: districts that receive or use more Class 2 water may differ systematically from other districts. Descriptive association is feasible now; causal “insurance value” requires a defensible source of variation and balanced outcome coverage.

Glossary

Allocation

The share of a contractual water class that USBR makes available in a year. It can be revised as conditions change.

Delivery

Water recorded as delivered through the system. It can differ from availability because of schedules, transfers, exchanges, carry-over, recharge operations, demand and infrastructure.

Acre-foot

A volume equal to one acre covered by one foot of water—about 325,851 US gallons or 1,233 cubic metres.

LULC

Land use / land cover. Here it describes the mapped 2023 crop and land-use category of each field unit.

Groundwater depth

The vertical distance from the land surface to measured groundwater at a monitoring point. Greater depth generally means water is farther below the surface.

Recharge

Water entering an aquifer. Managed recharge may use canals, basins or fields when water and suitable conditions are available.

Groundwater potential

A relative screening score built from physical themes. It is not the amount of groundwater available for pumping.

Source links and caveats are part of the analysis, not decorative footnotes.
